```{r}
#| label: setup

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

# Rotational Symmetry

Rotational symmetry of order \( n \) (cyclic group \( \mathbb{Z}_n \)) means a figure looks the same after rotation by \( 360^\circ / n \).

## R example: rotating a point

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "Points generated by successive 72° rotations (order 5)"

theta <- 2 * pi / 5
pts <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 0)
for (i in 1:4) {
  R <- matrix(c(cos(theta), -sin(theta), sin(theta), cos(theta)), 2, 2)
  newpt <- as.numeric(R %*% c(pts$x[i], pts$y[i]))
  pts <- rbind(pts, data.frame(x = newpt[1], y = newpt[2]))
}

ggplot(pts, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_path(color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x=0, y=0), aes(x,y), shape = 3, size = 3, color = "black") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.3, 1.3), ylim = c(-1.3, 1.3)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Order-5 rotational symmetry")
```

## p5.js: interactive rotational symmetry

```{=html}
<div id="rotational-sketch"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/p5@1.9.0/lib/p5.min.js"></script>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let n = 5;
  let angle = 0;
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    p.background(240);
    p.translate(200, 200);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      p.push();
      p.rotate(angle + i * p.TWO_PI / n);
      p.fill(100, 150, 220, 180);
      p.noStroke();
      p.ellipse(80, 0, 30, 30);
      p.pop();
    }
    angle += 0.01;
  };
}, document.getElementById("rotational-sketch"));
</script>
```

# Reflectional Symmetry

Mirror symmetry across a line (usually the vertical or horizontal axis).

## R example

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-cap: "A shape and its mirror image (outlines + light fill)"

base <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 1, 1.5, 1, 0),
  y = c(0, 0.5, 0, -0.5, 0)
)
mirror <- data.frame(x = -base$x, y = base$y)

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = base, aes(x, y), fill = "coral", alpha = 0.25, color = "coral", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = mirror, aes(x, y), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-2, 2), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## p5.js: draw with mirror symmetry

```{=html}
<div id="mirror-sketch"></div>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    if (p.mouseIsPressed) {
      let x = p.mouseX - 200;
      let y = p.mouseY - 200;
      p.stroke(0);
      p.strokeWeight(3);
      p.point(200 + x, 200 + y);
      p.point(200 - x, 200 + y); // vertical mirror
    }
  };
}, document.getElementById("mirror-sketch"));
</script>
<p><em>Click and drag to draw. The sketch mirrors your strokes across the vertical axis.</em></p>
```

# Dihedral Symmetry (\( D_n \))

Dihedral groups combine rotations of order \( n \) with reflections. These are the symmetries of regular polygons.

## R example: regular pentagon and its symmetries

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "Regular pentagon (D5 symmetry)"

n <- 5
angles <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n + 1)
poly <- data.frame(
  x = cos(angles),
  y = sin(angles)
)

ggplot(poly, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "gold", alpha = 0.6, color = "black") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Dihedral group D5")
```

## p5.js: kaleidoscope-style dihedral drawing

```{=html}
<div id="dihedral-sketch"></div>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let n = 6;
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    if (p.mouseIsPressed) {
      p.translate(200, 200);
      for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        p.push();
        p.rotate(i * p.TWO_PI / n);
        p.stroke(p.random(100, 200), p.random(100, 200), p.random(100, 200));
        p.strokeWeight(2);
        let x = p.mouseX - 200;
        let y = p.mouseY - 200;
        p.line(0, 0, x, y);
        p.line(0, 0, x, -y); // reflection
        p.pop();
      }
    }
  };
}, document.getElementById("dihedral-sketch"));
</script>
<p><em>Click and drag. The sketch applies both rotations and reflections of order 6.</em></p>
```

# Design Notes for Art Students

- **Rotational only** (\( \mathbb{Z}_n \)): swirling, pinwheel-like, no mirror lines.
- **Reflection only**: bilateral balance (faces, logos, architecture).
- **Dihedral** (\( D_n \)): the most common decorative symmetry (snowflakes, flowers, rose windows, tiles).

These geometric ideas become the constraints we later impose on iterative and random processes.
